sentence: Sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses, and it is usually caused by an infection.
The NHS describes it as common, and it usually clears up on its own within 4 weeks.
MedlinePlus explains that sinusitis results from an inflammatory reaction or an infection with a virus, bacteria or a fungus.
Sinusitis that lasts a long time is called chronic sinusitis.
One MedlinePlus page describes it as sinus swelling and symptoms lasting longer than 3 months.
Another MedlinePlus page describes it as lasting more than 12 weeks and says it can continue for months or even years.
note: MedlinePlus sinus infection page; the two pages word the length differently.

sentence: MedlinePlus says the symptoms of chronic sinusitis tend to be milder but last longer than those of a short infection.
The NHS lists pain and tenderness in the face, a blocked or runny nose and a reduced sense of smell as main symptoms.
Coloured mucus from the nose and a fever are also listed.
Headache, toothache and bad breath are other common symptoms.
In young children, irritability and trouble feeding can appear.
MedlinePlus lists pressure or pain in the face, a stuffy nose with discharge, cough, fever and headache.
It also lists mucus running down the back of the throat, known as postnasal drip.
note: MedlinePlus summary; term postnasal drip given by the search summary.

sentence: A GP can usually diagnose sinusitis from these symptoms, together with a look inside the nose.
MedlinePlus advises contacting a health care provider, such as a GP, if symptoms last beyond 10 to 14 days or if a fever develops.
note: MedlinePlus: contact a provider if symptoms last beyond 10 to 14 days or fever develops; GP named as the UK route by author.

sentence: The NHS says a cold or flu virus spreading to the sinuses from the upper airways is the usual cause.
Only a few cases involve bacteria.
MedlinePlus says blocked sinus openings or extra mucus can let germs multiply.
A deviated nasal septum, a nasal bone spur or nasal polyps may block the openings of the sinuses.
Several things are linked to a higher chance of sinusitis.
The NHS lists allergies, nasal polyps, smoking and a weakened immune system.
MedlinePlus adds allergic rhinitis, cystic fibrosis, attending day care and abnormal sinus structures.
It gives HIV and chemotherapy as reasons for a weakened immune system.
MedlinePlus says chronic sinusitis may be caused by bacteria or a fungus.
It adds that an inflammatory reaction, and not only an infection, can lead to sinusitis.
A GP can usually diagnose sinusitis from the symptoms and by looking inside the nose.
Imaging may be used if the diagnosis is unclear.
Referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist is considered for severe or repeated cases.
For self-care, the NHS suggests rest, plenty of fluids, pain relief and saline nasal rinses.
It also suggests avoiding allergy triggers and not smoking.
Decongestant sprays should not be used for more than a week, because longer use can make congestion worse.
A pharmacist or GP may suggest steroid or antihistamine nasal treatments.
NICE guideline NG79 aims to limit antibiotic use and reduce antibiotic resistance.
For people with symptoms for about 10 days or less, it advises against offering an antibiotic.
Antibiotics are still offered at any time to people who are very unwell, show signs of a more serious illness or are at high risk of complications.
The NHS says surgery is recommended only in some cases.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 if someone is very unwell, painkillers do not help or symptoms get worse, or the immune system is weakened.
A GP appointment is advised if there is no improvement after 7 days of treatment from a pharmacist or GP, none after 3 weeks of self-care, or the problem keeps coming back.
A GP may refer someone to an ENT specialist if symptoms persist after 3 months of treatment, if it keeps coming back, or if only one side of the face is affected.
Complications are very rare, according to MedlinePlus.
It lists an abscess, a bone infection, meningitis and infection of the tissue around the eye.
Swelling around the eye or face, blood-stained discharge from the nose or changes in vision need prompt medical review, through the GP the same day or NHS 111.
note: NHS summary and MedlinePlus; named route is the standard urgent route.
